title: Gathering Materials for the Temple
overview: Solomon makes a trade deal with Hiram, king of Tyre, for timber and skilled workers, and drafts huge labor crews to begin building the temple his father David had planned.

parts.label: Hiram's friendly greeting (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Tyre was a wealthy trading city on the coast north of Israel, and its king Hiram had been David's ally. Sending envoys to a new king was the normal way to renew a friendship between royal houses.

parts.label: Solomon's plan for the temple (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: Solomon explains that David's constant wars kept him from building, but now there is peace, and God had promised David that his son would build it. A temple "for the Name" of the LORD means a place where God's presence and reputation would be honored, not a house that could contain God.

parts.label: A request for cedar (v. 6)
parts.note: The cedar forests of Lebanon were famous, and Hiram's people, the Sidonians, were the region's expert loggers. Solomon offers to send his own men to work alongside them and to pay whatever wages Hiram asks.

parts.label: Hiram's trade deal (vv. 7-12)
parts.note: Hiram praises Israel's God, which may mean he worshiped the LORD or may simply be the polite way an ally honored a neighbor's god; interpreters are unsure. He agrees to float the logs down the coast as rafts in return for yearly shipments of wheat and olive oil for his court, and the two kings seal a formal treaty.

parts.label: Drafted workers (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: Solomon forced 30,000 Israelites into labor in Lebanon, rotating them so each spent one month away and two at home, while another 150,000 hauled and cut stone (a parallel account in 2 Chronicles 2 says these were foreigners living in Israel). This forced labor was a real burden, and later in 1 Kings resentment over it helps tear the kingdom apart.

parts.label: Foundation stones (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: Huge, costly blocks were quarried and carefully cut to form the temple's foundation. Builders from Israel, Tyre and Byblos, another coastal city, shaped the stone and timber together.

think: When a grand project depends on the hard, unchosen labor of many people, how do you weigh what it achieves against what it costs them?
